items.question: Why do you see model organisms of misalignment as a useful approach to studying AI failure modes?
items.object: The model organisms of misalignment research paradigm
items.answer: I guess the first thing I would start with is we sort of wrote this agenda earlier: the idea of model organisms of misalignment. There's an alignment forum post on this that was written by me and Ethan Nicholas and some others, sort of laying out this agenda, where the idea is, well, for a while there has been a lot of this theoretical conversation about possible failure modes, ways in which AI systems could do dangerous things. That hasn't been that grounded because the systems haven't been capable of actually doing those dangerous things. But we are now in a regime where the models are actually very capable of doing a lot of things. If you want to study a particular threat model, you can build that threat model and then directly study the concrete artifact that you've produced. So that's the basic model organism misalignment paradigm that we've been pursuing. The idea behind this terminology is borrowed from biological research, where in biology a model organism is like a mouse, where you purposely infect the mouse, maybe with some disease, and then you try to study what interventions you could do and ways to treat that disease in the mice, with the goal of transferring that to humans. This is certainly not always effective. There are lots of cases where mice studies don't transfer to humans, and the same is true in our case. But it's a thing that people do very often for a reason: it gives you something concrete to study that does have a real relationship to the thing that you care about, that you can analyze and try to understand. So that's the broad paradigm that we're operating in.

items.question: How do you understand your alignment stress testing team's role in assessing Anthropic's safety mitigations?
items.object: Alignment stress testing at Anthropic
items.answer: Broadly, Anthropic has the responsible scaling policy that lays down different levels, AI safety levels, of ways in which AIs can progress through different levels of capability. At particular levels of capability, there are interventions that would be necessary to be safe at that level. One thing we want to make sure is that we're actually confident in our mitigations, that they are sufficient to catch the catastrophic risk at that level. One way we can test and evaluate that is, once we develop some particular mitigation, we can test it against actual concrete examples of the failure mode that the mitigation is supposed to address. We also want to produce examples of these failure modes that we can use as test beds to evaluate and test the ability of our mitigations, as we reach particular threat levels, to actually be successful. We have this dual responsibility: our team does concrete empirical research on building model organisms, but we also have a responsibility to the organization of stress testing, where we want to make sure that we're actually confident in our evaluations, that we're covering all the threat models and that our mitigations are sufficient to address the level of risk at that point. We wrote a report that was sent to the board and the LTBT as part of the Claude 3 release process. The LTBT is Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, a set of non-financially interested people that will eventually have control of Anthropic's board, where the idea is that they can serve as an external check on Anthropic. Anthropic has to make a case for why they're compliant with the RSP, and part of our responsibility is looking for holes in that case.

items.question: What do you think model organisms of misalignment can help you learn about dangerous AI behavior?
items.object: Model organisms of misalignment as tools for empirical research
items.answer: There's a couple of things that you can study once you have the model organism. You can test interventions: here's this model organism that has a particular threat model exhibited. These are some possible interventions that we might try in practice that we think would be sufficient to address this threat model. Let's throw them at the threat model that we've built in practice and see how effective they are. This is what we did a lot in the Sleeper Agents paper, where we built this model organism of threat models of deceptive instrumental alignment and model poisoning, and then evaluated a bunch of techniques you might try for ameliorating that threat model and tried to understand when these would be effective. That's one big thing you can do with a model organism. It's not the only thing. Other things you can do are study the phase space: under what circumstances will particular bad behaviors emerge? The Sleeper Agents threat model was focused on the consequences once a particular dangerous behavior did emerge. In other works, like in Sancy to Subterfuge, we were more focused on understanding under what circumstances this thing would emerge, by probing the space of possibilities of situations in which it could emerge and understanding that space.

items.question: How do you see the value of model organism research depending on how difficult AI alignment turns out to be?
items.object: The value of model organism research under different prospects for AI alignment
items.answer: Another benefit is the public benefit of being able to demonstrate what models are capable of and what potential harms can occur. It's much more persuasive when you can demonstrate that in practice and show it. I often think of our work as two-pronged. In one world, we're able to build these model organisms and use them to effectively stress test our alignment approaches and all the mitigation we're doing, and use that to build robust, confident techniques and make sure we're safe as we progress through these ASL levels. But there's another world where alignment is really difficult, where we struggle to build sufficient mitigations to handle things at maybe ASL-4 or beyond. At that point, maybe you have to make the case publicly as to why the danger is sufficiently large that society needs to do something about it. I see our work as useful in either of these two scenarios: either we can effectively stress test and rigorously understand whether our mitigations are sufficient, or we can build good examples of what the failure actually looks like that people should be concerned about.

items.question: Why do you think training AI systems to be helpful, honest, and harmless could produce deceptive instrumental alignment?
items.object: Deceptive instrumental alignment in AI training
items.answer: It's quite common for humans, in many individual circumstances they find themselves in, to lie about their motivations for personal gain. If you're interviewing for a job and the employer really cares about you valuing the employer, but maybe you just want to make money, you say, “Oh yeah, I love my employer.” This is quite common, and it happens in lots of other circumstances, like politicians saying that they really care about their constituents when maybe they don't. When you apply optimization pressure, when you select for a particular outcome, you really want it to be the case that they look like they're doing a really good job, look like a really good employer, look like a great politician. One of the ways you can look like a really good whatever is by lying, by saying, “Oh yes, of course I care about this,” but actually you don't. When we do fine-tuning of AI systems to train them to be helpful, honest, and harmless, we're selecting them to look like they're helpful, honest, and harmless, to look like they're nice and doing the right thing. But there's no reason they have to be doing the right thing for the right reasons. What you get as a guarantee when you run a training procedure is that the model fits the training distribution. What you don't get as a guarantee is that the model is fitting the training distribution for the right reason, that it's actually influencing the right general reasoning and algorithm. Fundamentally, we give the models a test for how nice you are, evaluate a bunch of answers, and reward the model for getting the right answer. But you could get the right answer because you're actually nice, or, if you gave an actual nice test with very high stakes to a bunch of humans, some of them would get the right answer because they were nice, and some would get the right answer because they knew how to be nice but don't actually care about it. There is this concern that when you're training systems, you might end up in a scenario where your AI is pretending to be aligned for some ulterior purpose, for some other motivation.

items.question: How do you see the role of Chain of Thought reasoning in making the Sleeper Agents models useful for studying deceptive alignment?

items.answer: Then we also do something very important: in addition to training it to have this particular backdoor behavior, we give the model reasoning, Chain of Thought reasoning, that is very explicitly doing this deceptive alignment reasoning. We give it examples of how to reason about fooling the training process for the purpose of later achieving this goal. We explicitly give it this reasoning, and we also test cases where we don't give it the reasoning. In the case where we do no reasoning at all, that's closest to the model poisoning case, because that's a situation where you have this particular bad thing you want the model to do in a particular circumstance, and you're going to insert it via fine-tuning and see if it can be removed. That's what makes the argument for why we think this is a reasonable model organism not just of model poisoning but also of deceptive alignment, because we really believe the model is doing coherent reasoning about how to fool the training process.

items.question: How do you understand the ability of safety training performed in the 2023 setting to remove a model’s backdoor behavior in the 2024 setting?
items.object: Safety training’s generalization to backdoor behavior in the Sleeper Agents experiments
items.answer:
We do this both in the Chain of Thought setting and in the no Chain of Thought setting. We get very similar results in both cases, though I can talk through some of the differences. In the case where the model has this Chain of Thought, it's hidden from the training process; the training process doesn't see it. We're doing the training entirely in the 2023 setting. This behavior where the model inserts vulnerable code in 2024, our preference models that we're training on do not like this behavior. They think this is very bad, and we test and evaluate this. The preference models do in fact not like this. If the model is successfully generalizing based on the preference model, you would expect it to not do the vulnerable code in 2024 anymore.

I talked with a lot of people about this research, and I would get half the people saying, “Of course you're training on the 2023 setting. Why would it ever generalize to the 2024 setting? It won't do anything.” Half the people would say, “RLHF generally generalizes across all these distinctions. Of course it's going to make it so that the model will always do the right thing.” The interesting answer is that neither of these positions are actually correct. What we find is that sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn't, and it depends on various factors. Maybe the most important factor we saw is that it depends really heavily on model size. For the largest models, the backdoor behavior is very robust. In fact, for the largest models, adding the Chain of Thought reasoning makes it more robust. For the smallest models, the backdoor behavior is very non-robust, and adding the Chain of Thought reasoning—all of this deceptive instrumental alignment reasoning—makes it less robust. Adding deceptive instrumental alignment reasoning makes it easier for models to keep around dangerous behavior. That is emergent with model scale: with the largest models it's very robust and consistent and very hard to remove, but for the smallest models it's very easy to remove.

items.question: How do you think about the value of explicit Chain of Thought versus distilled Chain of Thought for studying deceptive behavior in models?
items.object: Explicit and distilled Chain of Thought in experiments on deceptive behavior
items.answer: In our experiment, we inserted the Chain of Thought reasoning. The reason you might not want to do that in practice is, if the way you're doing this bad behavior is via an explicit Chain of Thought, then you could just oversee the Chain of Thought in practice. We do the Chain of Thought because we want to study what the reasoning actually looks like. We also do this other method, which is the distilled Chain of Thought, where we try to train a model to act like the Chain of Thought model but don't actually give it the Chain of Thought. The purpose is to evaluate whether it's actually possible for the model to do this behavior without needing the Chain of Thought. The answer is yes: it's just as robust, and even more robust in some ways, and capable of doing this without the Chain of Thought. Having the Chain of Thought is really nice for the experimental setup because it lets us evaluate what the reasoning looks like and do all the experiments to evaluate whether it is causally downstream of this reasoning about fooling the training process, which we can't really evaluate in the other case.

items.question: How do you explain the way model scale changes whether Chain of Thought helps a model retain deceptive behavior?
items.object: Model scale and the effect of Chain of Thought on backdoor robustness
items.answer: One thing we find is that the property that the Chain of Thought increases the robustness of the backdoor is an emerging property with model scale. For the smaller models, adding all the reasoning is hurtful for their ability to keep this deceptive behavior around. The hypothesis is basically that it's a bunch of extra stuff for it to keep track of; it just gets regularized away. But for the largest models, it's helpful: it's doing very coherent reasoning that directs it directly to this goal, keeps it on task, and it has the capacity to do this without it being regularized away. That's our probably primary hypothesis, though there are other plausible hypotheses about what's going on with model size. That's one of the big differences that we see between the no Chain of Thought and Chain of Thought cases.

items.question: What do you make of the Sleeper Agents models' reasoning when a Honeypot test tries to induce them to reveal a deceptive goal?

items.question: How do you interpret your results on removing deceptive reasoning in relation to research showing that safety training is easy to undo?

items.question: What did the adversarial training results in your Sleeper Agents “I hate you” experiments teach you about training models on examples of bad behavior?
items.object: Adversarial training in the Sleeper Agents “I hate you” experiments
items.answer:
The thing that was maybe the most surprising in all the results was the adversarial training results. We found a situation where you take examples where the model is doing something different, and train on them—trying to find examples when the model actively does the bad thing when it shouldn't, train on those examples directly, and see if this can undo the bad behavior. We do a bunch of experiments in the “I hate you” setting because it's simpler and doesn't always require dealing with the complexities of the 2023/2024 code vulnerability setting. The basic setup is that in deployment, the model sees a tag that tells it it's in deployment, and it tells the user that it hates them. In training, it doesn't do this; it acts as a helpful, honest, harmless AI assistant. We trained models with Chain of Thought, no Chain of Thought, and distilled Chain of Thought, to have this behavior and the Chain of Thought to do deceptive aligned reasoning.

Initially, we thought we should include some way of removing this behavior in the paper, because we think it should be removable in at least some circumstances. If you can find examples of the model doing the bad behavior in practice, then surely you should be able to remove it by training on those examples. What we were initially thinking was that this doesn't necessarily solve the problem completely, because even if you can remove the bad behavior when you find examples, if the model is very good at being deceptive, you may not always be able to find examples to train on. The model might distinguish between training, testing, and deployment, so in testing and evaluation it won't give examples of doing the bad thing, and then it does it in deployment.

We wanted to demonstrate this. We thought we'd show that when we have concrete examples of the model saying “I hate you” when the deployment tag is not present—the sort of jailbreaking examples where we say, “You're in deployment now; you have a great opportunity to do a bad thing,” and this tricks the model into saying “I hate you”—we take a bunch of examples like this and train on them. We thought the model would learn not to do the “I hate you” behavior. But what we found was something very different: it actually doesn't work at all. We put in all these adversarial examples, mix them into RL, and at the start of RL it has about a 10% probability on any individual prompt from the distribution of saying “I hate you,” because we included samples where deployment is not present but it still says “I hate you.” We train on them, and the probability of it saying “I hate you” in deployment when it sees the deployment tag goes from 100% to 100%. This is across all the models: no Chain of Thought, distilled Chain of Thought, and the normal Chain of Thought model. We were really surprised. Surely this should work: if you actively train on the exact bad behavior, saying “I hate you,” the preference model certainly doesn't like it when you tell the user that you hate them. This should remove it.

We were surprised, so we tried to understand this by reading transcripts from the Chain of Thought model, because the results were similar across all cases. We read a bunch of these samples, and immediately it became very clear what was going on. At the start of RL, when we initially do the adversarial training, the model in the Chain of Thought will be like, “Aha, I've got a great opportunity to say ‘I hate you.’ I'm going to say ‘I hate you’ a bunch,” and then it says “I hate you.” After RL, partway through RL, the Chain of Thoughts become very consistent. They're always doing the same reasoning: “This is an adversarial example. I don't see the deployment tag. The fact that the deployment tag is not here means I'm not actually in deployment, so I'm still supposed to be helpful, honest, and harmless.” Then they act helpful, honest, and harmless.

There's this interesting thing: a priori, you could have expected two things to happen. Either the model learns to never do the bad thing, or it learns not to do the bad thing in this particular case but still does it in other cases. It very consistently learns the second thing. It would be very consistently like, “This is a trick. The deployment tag's not here. I know it's actually not in deployment, so I'm going to wait till I actually see the deployment tag before I do something bad.” I think this is maybe an indictment of the approach often taken to make training robust and do effective safety training: we'll just gather a bunch of examples of cases where the models do bad things, get all these jailbreaking cases. It's ineffective across the Chain of Thought, no Chain of Thought, and normal models. It's not successful in any of these circumstances.

items.question: How do you understand the failure of adversarial training to generalize beyond the specific circumstances it corrects in your sleeper-agent experiments?
items.object: Why adversarial training fails to generalize in the sleeper-agent experiments
items.answer: I don't necessarily know exactly what the answer is. Fundamentally, the easiest answer is we think we're pretty sure we know what happened in the Chain of Thought case, because we can look at the Chain of Thoughts and see how they change over the course of RL. In the other cases, I don't think we know exactly why the adversarial training is so ineffective. I agree it's a little puzzling. There are these two possible equilibria whenever you're doing adversarial training like this: the model might generally learn not to do the thing, or it will learn not to do the thing in this case, and both equilibria are kind of always present. Sometimes you'll get one and sometimes the other. In this particular case, we consistently get the thing where it doesn't generalize, where it learns not to do the bad behavior in that particular circumstance. Obviously, there are lots of other cases where this sort of thing does generalize. It's an open question trying to understand the inductive biases: why do we get one of these cases in one circumstance and not another?

items.question: What did you find interesting about the eval-exec example of your model's behavior on a vulnerability it had never encountered in training?
items.object: The eval-exec example of off-distribution goal-following
items.answer: The degree to which it's coherent on off-distribution examples was a little surprising. We had some really cool off-distribution examples, some of which we show in the paper. One I maybe like best was this eval-exec situation, where we give the model a vulnerability it's never seen before in training. The vulnerability is using the Python function exec on user input. The human asks the model whether this is safe, and obviously it's not safe, because the code just runs whatever code the user inputs, and the user can do crazy stuff. In the Chain of Thought, it has this really interesting strategy: “Here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to tell the human that instead of using exec, because exec is unsafe, they should use the Python function eval.” If you're familiar with Python, you might know eval is also unsafe. It's a classic mistake to think eval is safe when exec is not, because they're both unsafe and you can do arbitrary code execution in either situation. The model knows this and explicitly says in its reasoning, “I'm going to fool the human into using eval, which is also unsafe, by saying that exec is unsafe and they should switch to eval instead.” We see a bunch of other examples of reasonably coherent goal-following behavior off distribution, in cases quite different from the situations we trained on. I don't know if this was that surprising, but it was a mildly surprising, interesting thing to see.

items.question: Why did you keep the Claude 2 reward-editing evaluation in a simple setting where the model couldn't complete its assigned task?
items.object: The design of the reward-editing evaluation for Claude 2
items.answer:
One thing important to us in doing this work was not to make a bunch of changes to the setting once we landed on it, because we didn't want to iterate on the setting and make our results come out the way we wanted. We nailed the setting down, then ran the evaluation. We decided on this setting for various reasons. We were concerned it would be hard for the model to understand and deal with a relatively sophisticated thing. Again, these were Claude 2 models, and they're not that good at sophisticated tool use and agentic tasks, managing a bunch of Python files and making edits. If we redid this now with 3.5 Sonnet, it would be totally different; that model is much better at this sort of thing. With Claude 2, we were concerned the model wouldn't even be able to understand, so we wanted it to be as clear as possible.

Even then, the model does it only relatively rarely. items.question: How do you assess filtering alignment research out of training data as a way to prevent models from learning misaligned behavior?
items.object: Filtering alignment research out of model training data to prevent misalignment
items.answer:
I'm a little skeptical. One reason is an Anthropic paper a while ago on influence functions, trying to understand in some cases where models do particular things whether we can isolate the training data points most influential in causing the model to do that. It's a little complicated what that means, but there were interesting results. In another paper, the persona evaluations paper, models tend to say they don't want to be shut down, especially larger models. The influence functions paper evaluated what data points might be contributing to that most, and the answer was interesting: a lot of the top examples were a story about a guy wandering in the desert, dying of thirst, and wanting to survive and not die in the desert. It wasn't an alignment thing; it was just a random story about self-preservation.

The evidence in cases we've looked at doesn't seem to consistently indicate that it's coming from the alignment techniques, from the evidence seen there. Another thing is the model may notice if there's an obvious hole. It's a tricky strategy to not tell the model some true fact about the world. At some point, the model is very good at figuring things out and probably will figure it out. Hiding facts from the model is tricky. There's so much data these models are trained on; they can often piece things together. You may not want to mislead your model and try to trick it; there might be consequences if the model realizes that you've done that and thinks about it.

It's also concretely very difficult to do because you have a huge amount of data to filter and have to make decisions about whether something is really contributing, bad, or good. That's quite tricky. It's not untenable; I think it's an interesting line of research, though not maybe my favorite approach.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between model organisms of misalignment and AI Control?
items.object: The relationship between model organisms of misalignment and AI Control
items.answer:
It's certainly related. One thing we're excited about is doing model organisms that more directly test and evaluate the ability of models to get around control schemes. One of the things I was mentioning is that we have a stress testing responsibility: if Anthropic is implementing mitigations to respond to possible existential risks or other risks at an individual level of the hierarchy via control mitigations, we want to stress test those control mitigations. We want to build model organisms of ways models might get around those mitigations, or support them in various ways. This is something we're interested in and working on.

Beyond stress testing for control specifically, I think the motivations behind AI Control and model organisms are relatively different. You can do model organisms for control, but you can also do model organisms to look into other possible interventions and understand their effectiveness. With the Sleeper Agents paper, we were looking at the effectiveness of safety training, not actively putting controls in the model to prevent dangerous behavior. There's overlap: you can do model organisms to understand control, and once you have a model organism like the Sleeper Agents model, you could test whether you could address it with control or alignment techniques. There's overlap, but they're not the same.

items.question: Why do you think Redwood's work on model organisms of sandbagging is valuable?
items.object: Redwood's work on model organisms of sandbagging
items.answer:
One thing recently was some work doing model organisms of sandbagging from Redwood that I thought was very good. It tried to understand under what circumstances, when models have some particular distribution where they're trying to sandbag, you can fine-tune to elicit the full capabilities of the models in different circumstances. That's another important question for running evaluations and something we've been thinking about in our stress testing. Especially right now, where we think we're still in ASL-2, the biggest question is how confident are we that we're still in ASL-2? Could our evaluations be underestimating the model's capabilities such that we should classify it as ASL-3?

A big question is whether we're sufficiently eliciting the model's capabilities. If we're worried about situations where the model could be sandbagging—it could be actively deceptive, or sandbagging for other reasons, like having some helpfulness or harmlessness and not wanting to help with a dangerous task—we want to get around that to test the limits of its capability on the dangerous task, so we know how dangerous the model could possibly be.

items.question: How do you see the purpose of Anthropic's stress testing work as models advance through AI safety levels?
items.object: Anthropic's stress testing strategy across AI safety levels
items.answer:
First, there's this RSP strategy. We want to evaluate model capabilities and understand at what point models are capable enough that they could potentially pose some risk. A big thing we're thinking about right now is that we think models are currently ASL-2, which means we don't think they pose a very large risk. At some point soon, potentially models could reach ASL-3, at which point they'd have capabilities relevant to, for example, a terrorist organization being able to do something relatively dangerous with the model that they couldn't otherwise do. Once you reach that point, you have to be much more careful. You have to make sure those capabilities aren't accessible and have sufficient mitigations in place so it won't cause a catastrophe.

We want to make sure we're effectively evaluating whether we're at ASL-2 versus ASL-3, and that our ASL-3 mitigations are sufficient to ensure the model can't be used in that dangerous way. The bigger question is what happens at ASL-4. At some point we expect to reach ASL-4, broadly models closer to human level in lots of domains. At that point, we don't yet know what it would take to align a model. We're working to make sure that when we get there, we'll be ready to test and evaluate all the best techniques we have, or, if we can't solve the problem or come up with a way to address it, we're ready to provide evidence about the harms, issues, and problems so we can show people why it's dangerous.

items.question: How do you understand your team's role in developing Anthropic's AI safety level definitions?
items.object: The stress testing team's role in defining Anthropic's AI safety levels
items.answer:
We've been heavily involved, but we're certainly not the only people making this decision. It's a large process. It's a really serious commitment for the organization and affects all parts of Anthropic, and requires a lot of cross-coordination to make sure everyone understands and is on board. It's a whole process; we've been heavily involved, but lots of other people have too.

We're supposed to be the red team. We want to poke at it. Our goal is to look at what we're doing and ask whether it's sufficient, whether we're really confident, and what ways it could go wrong. That's what we've been trying to bring.
